_meta.note: THE LOOM v1 — Adam's gavel 2026-11-03: all nine gap skeletons approved, name stands. Architecture per E_E_Loom_Plot_Audit_2026-11-03.md: skeleton × axes (factored, not flat), twist deck, subplot deck (the being-vs-themself home), the Flip, drama/comedy register (GMG p.15), genre skins after GMG p.56 'Table: Scenarios According to the Six Scales' (archetype labels genericized for the public tool — restoring the book's franchise touchstones is a data edit). Every word original; S. John Ross's Big List (GMG p.16's cited resource) was audited for structure only. v0.9.1: per-skeleton glosses + the tutorial + the acknowledgement in professional form (full citation, storefront pointer, no-affiliation note).

skeletons.name: The Taking
skeletons.engine: The party must obtain something that someone — or something — does not want them to have.
skeletons.tmpl: The party must take {prize}. Between them and it stands {opposition}. They will come {method}.

opt.f: an object of power that will not stay quiet
a person held behind walls, law, and better locks than either
knowledge that exists in exactly one place
a living creature that others would cage, milk, or kill
a deed, a title — ownership of the ground itself
a guardianship sworn, bound, and long prepared for exactly this
rival claimants on the same road, racing the same clock
the rightful owner — alerted, lawful, and well-loved
no enemy at all but the land, which keeps its treasures the hard way
by shadow — unseen, unsigned, and never suspected
by storm — over the walls and through the gate
by the silver tongue — invited in, and welcome
by purse and paper, if the asking price can be survived
at speed — first past the post takes all

skeletons.gloss: The oldest engine in the hobby, and still the most forgiving for a new GM: the party knows what it wants from scene one. Prepare the prize’s home in loving detail — the fun lives in the approach. Note how the Method thread sets the session’s whole flavor: shadow runs on tension, storm on dice, the silver tongue on roleplay.

skeletons.name: The Hunt
skeletons.engine: Something out there must be found — and what happens at the finding is the whole question.
skeletons.tmpl: The party hunts {quarry}. The trail is {trail}. The commission says: {intent}.

opt.f: a fugitive who knows exactly why they run
someone taken — or someone who walked away, which is worse
a beast already a legend in three counties
a quarry who does not yet know they are hunted
hours old and still warm
years cold, kept alive by one stubborn witness
fresh, obvious — and laid by someone who wants followers
alive, whatever it costs
stopped, either by restricted means or by any means
found and watched — and above all, not spooked

skeletons.gloss: Prep the trail as a chain of scenes, each ending in a pointer to the next. The Quarry thread quietly decides your ENDING — a cornered fugitive, a grateful victim, and a magnificent beast ask for three very different final scenes, so know which one you’re building toward.

skeletons.name: The Vigil
skeletons.engine: Something precious persists only while the party stands over it.
skeletons.tmpl: The party keeps {charge} — {posture}. The catch in the watch: {flaw}.

opt.f: a person marked for death by professionals
a thing whose worth corrupts its own protectors
a line on the map that must not be crossed in one or either direction
a secret that must outlive its usefulness
on the moving road, where every mile deals a new hand
behind fixed walls, where the enemy chooses the hour
from the shadows, guarding a charge who mustn't know
the briefing was wrong about what is coming
the charge fights the protection at every turn
the threat is already inside the perimeter

skeletons.gloss: Protection plots put the GM on offense: you schedule the threats, the players improvise the answers. Decide in advance when and how each probe of their defenses comes. The Flaw thread is the story — without it this is just a quiet night of guard duty.

skeletons.name: The Riddle
skeletons.engine: The truth exists; everything else is in the way.
skeletons.tmpl: {tense} The matter at hand: {subject}. The deeper obstacle: {obstruction}.

opt.f: The deed is done — name the hand that did it.
The harm is happening now — trace it to its source before the next stroke.
The scheme is still forming — prove it before proof becomes hindsight.
a death that arithmetic says was impossible
a phenomenon that breaks a rule everyone trusted
a disappearance with too many clean explanations
something the party themselves did — and cannot / don't remember
a power that prefers the mystery exactly as it is
witnesses who fear the answer more than the crime
planted evidence that lies on purpose

skeletons.gloss: Build the truth FIRST — what actually happened, who knows what — then lay clues backward from it. Kindness rule for new GMs: every fact the party must learn should have at least three different clues pointing at it; players will miss one, mangle the second, and triumph over the third, generally speaking. This type of scenario can become almost exclusively skill checks, with an unmasking that may or may not entail a climactic final scene.

skeletons.name: The Purge
skeletons.engine: A place has been claimed by something that must be reclaimed.
skeletons.tmpl: The party must cleanse {infestation}. The catch: {key}. The difficulty: {stake}.

opt.f: a haunting grown bold enough to collect rent and require eviction
a breach that leaks horrors into the characters' world
a nest dug deep, where the maps go blank
a cult whose roots secrete corruption under a respectable facade
it cannot be fought until it is understood
cutting the visible growth does nothing — find the root
it must be starved of what feeds it — and what feeds it is precious to both sides
the party needs this place habitable by nightfall
the blight is spreading along lines only just becoming visible
innocents still live inside it — collateral damage entails degrees of failure

skeletons.gloss: A site-based scenario: map the place, seed it with signs, and let the dread accumulate room by room. The Key thread is doing quiet work for you — it forces an investigation beat before the violence, which is exactly the pacing a versatile scenario wants.

skeletons.name: The Crossing
skeletons.engine: Between the party and safety lies distance that fights back.
skeletons.tmpl: The obstacle: {trap}. The way out: {exit}. Carried along the way: {burden}.

opt.f: stranded off the edge of every map they trusted
taken, held, and inventoried
aboard a conveyance that no longer answers to its passengers
facing a gauntlet that must be run because going around it is either worse or impossible
repair the way home with what the wreck left behind
break the walls at the one hour they can be broken
outlast — rescue is coming, if they can still be found and survive the interim
reach the far side on foot, through all of it
wounded who cannot walk and will not be left
a thing that must also survive the crossing
pursuers who know the ground better

skeletons.gloss: Here the map itself is the antagonist, so prepare terrain, weather, and distances the way you’d stat a villain. Track supplies and rest honestly — resource pressure is the plot. This is the base plotline where being(s)-vs-nature gets to shine.

skeletons.name: The Battle Line
skeletons.engine: Two forces, one piece of ground, and the party is where the lines meet.
skeletons.tmpl: The party's part: {side}. The point of contention: {ground}. What the plan does not know: {wrinkle}.

opt.f: take it, before the enemy makes it unbreakable
hold it, until relief or new orders
a bridge, a gate, a pass — the only way through
a compound built by someone who expected this day would come
open country à la “no man’s land”, with innocents between the lines
a vessel underway, where retreat means the water / void
the intelligence underneath the plan is wrong
relief will come — if anyone lasts long enough to signal it
the enemy is not here for the ground, but for something hidden in it

skeletons.gloss: The set-piece skeleton: stat the ground as carefully as the forces, because cover, chokepoints, and fallback lines are what the players will actually play with. For maximum pressure, spring the Wrinkle mid-fight, not before — it exists to break a plan that was working.

skeletons.name: The Game
skeletons.engine: The party enters a contest with rules — and discovers that the rules are skewed.
skeletons.tmpl: The arena: {arena}. The rot in it: {corruption}. Riding on the outcome: {stake}.

opt.f: a tournament of arms, skill, or speed
a court where protocol is the weapon and a fork can be a scandal
a failing enterprise the party must run — and redeem
a wager that began as a joke and grew teeth
someone is cheating, and well
the prize is not what the posters promise
losing, it turns out, is lethal
standing — doors open here, or close forever
a life rides on the outcome, and not a volunteer's
the party's cover — winning IS the disguise

skeletons.gloss: Run the arena as rounds with visible standings between them, and make sure every hero’s talents get an event — the bard and aristocrat can belong at this tournament as much as the fighter and tactician do. The Skew thread turns a rule into a plot the moment someone notices it.

skeletons.name: The Squeeze
skeletons.engine: Someone owns the party's obedience — for now.
skeletons.tmpl: The compromising detail: {leverage}. The other party's ultimatum: {demand}. The way out: {out}.

opt.f: a hostage dear enough to end every argument
a secret that would unmake one of them
a debt or a crime manufactured to fit
a slow poison, and a timetable of antidotes
a theft they would refuse at any price
the betrayal of someone who trusts them
silence — merely watch it happen and say nothing
break the hold at its anchor
find the squeezer's own master, and trade up
comply to the letter — and find out what/if compliance delivers

skeletons.gloss: A pressure plot — talk tone with your table first, because coercion (what might erroneously be termed “railroading”) aimed at the heroes lands harder than a sword ever does. The payoff that makes it worthwhile: the turn, the session where the squeezed become the squeezers. The best squeeze scenarios build toward that potential for reversal from the first scene.

skeletons.name: The Serpent
skeletons.engine: The threat is inside the walls, wearing a trusted face.
skeletons.tmpl: The compromised territory: {nest}. The spy or assassin: {serpent}. The political twist: {bind}.

opt.f: the party's own patron's court
an allied house that must not be insulted
the expedition itself, one day from the trailhead
a dogmatic order whose faith forbids the very suspicion
a traitor selling the inside to the outside
a claimant thinning the succession one accident at a time
an impostor, almost word-perfect in a borrowed life
an open accusation shatters the alliance whether right or wrong
the likeliest suspect is the best-loved
suspicion has already landed — on the party

skeletons.gloss: Bookkeeping wins this one: keep a private ledger of who knows what, and what each clue would reveal to a careful reader. Give the serpent moves the players can almost catch. The Bind matters — a wrong accusation should cost something real, or suspicion is free and the tension dies.

skeletons.name: The Table
skeletons.engine: The war is optional; prudent diplomacy may yet prevail.
skeletons.tmpl: At the table: {parties}. The party's leverage: {leverage}. Working against the peace: {spoiler}.

opt.f: two powers one incident from open war
houses feuding past all memory of the cause
a city above, and something older beneath it
labor and master — and the harvest will not wait
both sides privately want a thing only the party can fetch
a secret that would collapse one side's case, held in trust
the true deadline / stakes, which only the party knows
a faction that profits handsomely from failure
an old wound neither delegation will speak aloud
the party's own flag: one side cannot trust it, and so cannot hear the warning it carries

skeletons.gloss: Stat the delegations as interests, not hit points: what each party needs, wants, and will walk away over. Let the players discover those three layers through play. The Spoiler thread is your action valve — when the talking needs a jolt, the peace’s enemies can happily provide one.

skeletons.name: The Sting
skeletons.engine: The lie is the weapon; the party is the lie.
skeletons.tmpl: The target of the operation: {mark}. The nature of the deception: {con}. The thread that may unravel it: {unravel}.

opt.f: a tyrant the law cannot reach
a swindler grown fat on the savings of the small
an institution armored in clerks and paper
an enemy spymaster who trades in exactly this
a borrowed identity with a short shelf life
a counterfeit prize too good to verify
an omen manufactured to order
the long game — trust built carefully, to be spent all at once
a face from the past who knows the real names
the mark is running a game of their own
the innocent bystanders are getting invested

skeletons.gloss: Plan the con in phases — the hook, the build, the shut-out, the take — and then expect your players to improvise sideways out of all of them; the plan existing is what makes the improvisation feel brilliant. The friendliest scenario to a comedy register in the whole Loom.

skeletons.name: The Seven
skeletons.engine: The storm is coming, and the village cannot stop it; the party is their only hope.
skeletons.tmpl: The one(s) in need of protection: {ward}. The one(s) coming to get them: {storm}. The means at hand: {means}.

opt.f: a village square in the storm's path
a caravan that must winter where it stands
a quarter the law has formally forgotten
raiders who keep a schedule
a creature that returns with the season
hired blades with a deadline and a ledger
training hands that have only ever held tools
fortifying with nothing but what is already here
uniting neighbors who hate each other almost enough to lose

skeletons.gloss: The preparation IS the adventure: training montages, fortification projects, and the ward’s people becoming names the party cares about. Spend two-thirds of your table time before the storm arrives — the showdown only matters because of who’s standing in it.

skeletons.name: The Deluge
skeletons.engine: The catastrophe has gone beyond threat; it is in progress.
skeletons.tmpl: The element(s) to be faced: {catastrophe}. The party's part: {role}. The truth underneath: {truth}.

opt.f: water rising faster than the ground can climb
fire taking the streets block by block
the earth itself opening old accounts
a great engine — or a great working — failing toward ruin
get them out — all of them, in the time there is
hold one line so that others can run
reach the heart of it, and make it stop
it was no accident
the rescue is somebody's cover for a harvest
this was the dress rehearsal — and the real one is yet forthcoming

skeletons.gloss: Run it on clocks: the fire spreads at noon, the bridge goes at dusk. Offer more emergencies than the party can answer and let triage be the drama — who they couldn’t save is the scene they’ll remember. The Realization thread can turn a disaster one-shot into a campaign hook.

skeletons.name: The Long Night
skeletons.engine: The night is long, and for some it may be their last; survival is the victory condition.
skeletons.tmpl: The unknown threat: {horror}. The hunting ground: {ground}. The chance for survival: {hope}.

opt.f: it hunts by rules nobody has survived long enough to learn
it wears the faces of the already-taken
it seemingly cannot be killed outright — only outlasted
sealed in with it, by accident or by design
a night that will not end until some condition is met
a circle of safety shrinking by the hour
first light, if everyone holds
one door, one window, one hour — out
its one rule or weakness, learnable at a terrible price

skeletons.gloss: Horror asks for consent before it asks for dice: agree with your table on lines and limits first (the GMG’s horror tools, and the Minds rules, are built for exactly this register). Then ration everything — light, ammunition, safe corners — and remember the monster’s rule / weakness is the real treasure of the night.

skeletons.name: The Reckoning
skeletons.engine: The verdict is coming; yet the truth and the verdict are not the same thing.
skeletons.tmpl: In the dock: {accused}. The source of the accusation: {court}. The crooked timber: {truth}.

opt.f: one of the party's own
a friend whose innocence is obvious — and inadmissible
an enemy guilty of everything except this
a stranger nobody else will stand for
the law — rigid, slow, and mostly-but-not-necessarily honest
a noble's whim wearing a robe
ordeal or trial by combat, as the old ways demand
the mob, which has already voted
the verdict has been purchased in advance
the real culprit watches from the gallery
acquittal is possible — at a price aimed squarely at the party

skeletons.gloss: Half the fun is procedure: let the players gather evidence, brief witnesses, and then ARGUE — as advocates, as the accused, as character witnesses with checkered pasts (keeping in mind Knowledge (Civics) is the typical skill for lawyering / litigation). Decide early what the court will actually weigh, so the verdict feels earned rather than assigned.

skeletons.name: The Throne
skeletons.engine: The order of things is in flux for the leadership — or the party.
skeletons.tmpl: The leadership in question: {regime}. The pain point: {lever}. The consequences of regime change: {price}.

opt.f: a usurper whose paperwork is immaculate
an occupier settling in to stay
a council rotted quietly from within
a crown failing, with no agreed-upon heir
an heir in hiding who may not want finding
an army three payrolls in arrears
a people one public spark from rising
written proof of the regime's founding crime
revolutions eat their firstborn — plan the aftermath
the likeliest successor is worse
order will fall faster than it can be rebuilt, and winter is coming

skeletons.gloss: Campaign-scale by nature: run the factions as characters with agendas that advance between sessions, whether or not the party is watching. The Price thread is your theme — a revolution plot is really a question about what order is worth, asked with swords.

twists.t: The clock is wrong — the deadline everyone planned around is sooner than believed, or it was never real.
The patron's true goal is not the stated commission; the party is the errand inside someone else's plot.
Two of the opposing forces are at war with each other — exploit the seam, or be crushed in it.
The objective is already gone when the party arrives; someone was faster, and they left a message.
Success springs the real trap: what the party accomplishes is exactly what a hidden power needed done.
An enemy from a past adventure holds the one key — and knows precisely what it is worth.
The party's reputation has arrived ahead of them, and it is problematic in a dangerous direction.
The weather — or the world — turns mid-adventure, and the board is suddenly a different game.
A rival party is on the same job for a different employer, and they are not incompetent.
One of the supposed victims is a quiet beneficiary of the villainy.
The lawful authority is the obstacle: what must be stopped is, technically, perfectly legal.
What the party learns must be kept from their own side, at least until the worst possible moment.
An innocent attaches to the party at the worst time, and they cannot be parked anywhere safe.
The supernatural turns out mundane — or the mundane explanation is itself the cover for the real haunting.
Mid-adventure, the employer dies, vanishes, or recants — the commission is suddenly an orphan.
The only road to success runs through a place one of the party swore never to enter again.

subplots.d: A power or prize within easy reach, costing a little more of the hero each time it is used. (The Mutation Scale's drawbacks can give this one real teeth in E&E.)
An allegiance pulls against the party's course — quietly at first, then on a day when both masters call at once.
An oath taken long ago, certain to come due at the least convenient hour of the main plot.
A curse, mutation, or appetite that grows with every use; the hero's strength and their doom minted on two sides of the same coin.
The horrors witnessed are keeping a ledger. (The Minds/sanity rules adjudicate this one natively.)
Someone once saved this hero's life. The bill arrives mid-plot, payable immediately, in kind.
A peer, possibly even a nemesis, who measures everything against this hero — helping, competing, and keeping score toward some final reckoning.
Something left behind — a farm, a family, a post — deteriorates a little with every week spent adventuring.
A hidden past the main plot keeps threatening to drag into the light.
The present plot rhymes with an old failure. Does the hero have the experience and intestinal fortitude to rise to the challenge this time?

registers.drama: Played straight (GMG p.15): consequences are real and the tension is the engine — let the quiet moments breathe.
registers.comedy: Played for laughs (GMG p.15): outrageous moments are expected, reactions run extreme, and hijinks are a legitimate tactic — escalate boldly.

acts.d: Introduce the premise through an NPC with a face and a want; secure the buy-in before the first door closes behind the party. (GMG pp.29-30)
The reveal that turns a job into a story — the first comfortable assumption breaks.
Pursue the objective into rising stakes; let subplots sprout from what the party does on the side. Usually the longest act.
The crisis — all seems lost, or the true antagonist finally shows their hand.
The uphill final confrontation; by its end, answer every question Act One asked. Usually the shortest act.

flip: THE FLIP — run it from the far side: the party is not driving this plot but defending against it, swept up in it by accident, hired to enable it, or the very thing it is aimed at. Every skeleton above inverts.

In measuring its breadth, the Loom’s designers gratefully studied S. herring.d: the adventure the party was offered is not the adventure they are in. Run the façade honestly through Act I — its hook, its patron, its stakes are real enough to bleed for — and let the truth surface at the first big reveal. Seed two clues early; a twist no one could have caught is a trick, not a story.

home.d: weave the premise into that hero’s own history — their hometown, their mentor, their debt, the name they stopped using — and let the party discover mid-stride whose story this really is.

fate.homeHerring: Rarest weave of all: a quest wearing a face from a hero’s own past — and the face is a mask.
